::: {.bs-editorial-lead}
The first version of my mark was the kind of idea that can begin as a sketch on a napkin: two A's reduced until they became one symbol. The useful lesson is not the final image. It is how the identity changed as I kept drawing, testing, removing, and adding meaning.
:::

## A personal logo should stay simple

My original AA mark was thin, angular, and easy to draw by hand.

![The original AA mark, first developed with pen and paper.](../assets/lore/logo-redesign/01-original-monogram.webp){fig-alt="The original thin, angular AA personal mark."}

Later I made the strokes heavier and curved the cross-arms.

![The revised AA mark with heavier strokes and curved cross-arms.](../assets/lore/logo-redesign/02-curved-monogram.webp){fig-alt="A heavier AA monogram with curved cross-arms."}

The curve feels more supportive than a straight bar. It can suggest an arch, a truss, an umbrella, part of a circle, an arrow, or the leading edge of a kite. Those references matter to me, but the logo does not need to explain all of them to everyone who sees it.

That is the point of a **personal logo**. It should be simple, memorable, reproducible, and recognizable at a small size. It should represent you without trying to tell your entire life story.

## Identity can change without rejecting where it came from

I was raised Catholic, and I still think of myself as a disciple of Jesus. That formation is part of me, but I do not need religion to be the organizing identity of a public educational site.

In Canada today, Catholic identity is not something I need a logo to defend, and I also do not want a public mark to be read as alignment with extreme religious or political positions. I would rather carry forward the values that matter to me, including service, care, humility, community, responsibility, and connection, while leaving room to work and learn with people whose beliefs are different from mine.

That helped push the mark away from being read too literally as a religious symbol and toward forms that could connect more broadly: structure, motion, shelter, direction, growth, and place.

## The black-and-white experiments

Once I moved from paper into digital tools, I deliberately explored too many ideas. Some were useful logo studies. Some became abstract art instead of logos. That distinction was helpful.

::: {.commons-logo-gallery}
![A chronological gallery of AA and Commons identity studies, beginning with the curved AA mark, moving through black-and-white geometric experiments, then lighthouse, leaf, root, wave, and colour studies before the current emblem.](../assets/lore/logo-redesign/05-logo-redesign-gallery.webp){fig-alt="Chronological gallery of twelve logo and emblem studies."}
:::

The black-and-white studies forced me to look at shape without depending on colour, texture, glow, or shading. Some of the circular and mirrored versions are interesting images, but they are closer to abstract art. If a design becomes unreadable at favicon size or depends on visual effects to work, it is probably not doing the job of a logo anymore.

## From a personal logo to a Commons emblem

The larger symbol is doing a different job. It represents **Technology Commons**, not just me, so it can carry more information than the AA logo.

The current emblem combines several ideas:

- the **AA structure** represents my authorship and support for the Commons
- the **lighthouse** connects to Port Credit Secondary School and suggests guidance and stewardship
- the **rocket-like upward form** connects the identity to science, technology, engineering, and aspiration
- the **water** connects to Port Credit, flow, movement, and learning
- the **roots** suggest heritage, growth, and a foundation that can exist even below the visible waterline
- the enclosing **circle** makes the image read as a shared organizational emblem rather than only a personal monogram

The lighthouse, leaves, roots, waves, and light did not arrive at once. Early versions added too much. Other versions became so simple that they lost the character I wanted. The current version sits between those extremes.

## Watching the identity iterate

::: {.commons-logo-progression}
![Animated progression from the AA mark through geometric studies and lighthouse iterations to the current Technology Commons emblem.](../assets/lore/logo-redesign/06-logo-redesign-progression.gif){fig-alt="Animated sequence showing the logo progressing from a simple AA mark to the current Commons emblem."}
:::

The animation makes the design process easier to see. The identity does not jump from one answer to another. It accumulates ideas, rejects some of them, and then simplifies again.

For students, that is the part worth copying. Start with a mark you can draw. Make several versions. Keep the rejected ideas. Test everything in black and white and at small size. Then decide whether you are making a **personal logo**, which should remain compact, or an **emblem for an organization, product, project, or community**, which may have room to carry a larger story.

The first sketch and the final emblem matter. Most of the design happened between them.
